spontaneous_story_understanding: The pandemic depressed oil demand and both benchmarks. According to the attributed EIA explanation, constrained storage at inland Cushing collided with the approaching May futures contract expiration: holders unable to receive oil needed to sell, while few buyers could accommodate barrels. That produced the extraordinary one-day WTI negative price. The broad slump persisted, but the negative observation and huge Brent–WTI gap were brief.
relationship_understanding: Chart1 distinguishes a common oil-price slump from a WTI-specific extreme and subsequent reconvergence. Chart2 distinguishes the negative daily observation from positive weekly and monthly averages. The prose supplies geographical and contract context for these relationships and explicitly says the plotted prices do not test the causal explanation.
what_prose_adds_or_changes: The prose names EIA as source, defines spot price and negative price, expands WTI and explains Cushing versus seaborne Brent. It explains why 6 January was selected: the annual peak for both. It supplies a full-record scope for the only-negative-day claim, which the short chart window could not establish alone. It adds the pandemic/storage/contract-expiry account, a distinct futures settlement figure of minus $37.63, and historical comparisons showing Brent nearly at its record low the next day and a lower WTI monthly average in 1998. My chart-only reading of a broad decline plus a transient WTI-specific event remains; the economic mechanism is newly supplied by prose.
uncertainty_and_unanswered_questions: The account moves from physical spot pricing to forced sales of a futures contract, then explains near the end that those prices measure different things. I understand the proposed connection but still want a clear explanation of how the expiring futures contract transmitted pressure to the displayed spot quote. The actual extent of full or committed storage and the reason conditions eased enough by the next day are not shown. The historical claims and attribution are assertions in the prose at this stage, not independently checked. The title's 'one place' and sentence 'One price did' sound broader than the evidence from two benchmarks can establish. Weekly averaging conventions remain unspecified, although the chart alt text identifies EIA weekly averages. The duplicate main title is an obvious presentation defect. All chart content was readable.
